2610.36141.title: A Model to Map Brown Dwarf Companions to White Dwarfs in Partial Secondary Eclipse

figures.caption: Figure 1: The best-fit light curve (blue) to the phase curve and transit data of WD 1202 (black points with error bars), integrated across 0.6–5.3 $\upmu$m. The data have been normalized to a reference median flux count of $\approx 13589.74$ $e^{-}$ s-1. The inset light curve plot shows a zoom-in to secondary eclipse, with the data excluded from the initial phase curve fit in grey. The shades of blue denote the 68th and 95th percentiles of the extrapolated light curves in eclipse. On top of the inset is a diagram showing a possible secondary eclipse geometry for the system, using the maximum-likelihood estimate for the impact parameter and relative radii. The bottom panel shows the residuals scaled to the model uncertainties, which have been inflated by a constant factor of $\approx 1.4$ from those calculated in the reduction. The error inflation factor is treated as a free parameter in our model.

Figure 2: The first several components of the phase-only and full-phase eigenbases for WD 1202. The main plot shows the fraction of variance explained as a function of the index of the eigenbasis component (eigenmode); this is equivalent to the eigenvalue (see Section III.3). The phase-only variance fractions are offset by two orders of magnitude for visual clarity. Inset plot (b) shows the light curves from each pure eigenmode for the phase-only eigenbasis, with colors corresponding to the numbers on the variance plot. Insets (c)–(d) show the corresponding light curves for the full-phase eigenbasis, with the grey shaded region denoting the time interval of secondary eclipse. Inset (d) shows the structure of the eigencurves within secondary eclipse (grey shading removed for clarity). The first 4 components (“eigenmodes”) appear similar to those of the phase-only eigenmodes, indicating most of the signal remains in the rotation at low harmonic degrees. Starting at the 5th eigenmode and higher, we see a concentration of brightness fluctuations along the path of occultation by the WD host. These modes are super-positions of phase-like and eclipse-like modes. As we approach the higher modes, the eclipse signal begins to dominate as brightness variations in the occulted region are able to produce more variance (signal) in the light curve than including longitudinal bands at increasing wavenumbers.

Each light curve is normalized to the $Y_{0,0}$ component of the map that produces it. A pair of dotted black lines denote the latitude range of the path of the host during secondary eclipse, here computed for the $b\approx 0.64$ orbital geometry. The statistically-preferred fit uses 9 eigenmodes and is shown in green. In the inset, we show the contribution of each mode relative to the mean brightness (constant term). We highlight a low-order fit in blue and a high-order fit in brown. In between, the highlighted colored modes correspond to where we gain structures that impart appreciable contribution to the flux in the occulted region. (f): The occultation asymmetry metric g, as defined in Equation 15, is plotted across the day-side longitudes in the upper row for a selection of model fits by number of eigenmodes. The true value of g for the dipole map is shown as a black horizontal line.

The upper left panel shows the statistical metric, the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC, as described in Section III.4), as a function of the number of eigenmodes. Note that the colors of selected eigenmodes correspond to those shown in Figure 3. For the dipole test, we find a minimum (optimal) value at 9 eigenmodes, as indicated by the triangle icon pointing to the minimum at zero. The penalized fit is then selected at the $\alpha$ whose MSE matches that of the BIC-preferred eigenmapping fit, the magnitude of the penalty term used in the complexity-penalized model. p is the exponent of the penalty that controls the prior on how the harmonic power spectrum falls off with increasing degree $\ell$. The initial approach is to fix p at a value of 2, which yields second-order Tikhonov regularization. To show that the model can converge to the true map in this simple example, we show a case of a stricter penalty exponent ($p=4$).

2610.36141.abstract: Eclipse mapping is a well-established technique for constraining the spatial emission of hot Jupiter exoplanets. Brown dwarfs in ultra-short orbits around white dwarfs are an analog to hot Jupiters that can only ever be eclipsed within a limited range of latitudes. We adapt the eigenmapping method to disentangle the signals from the ever- and never-occulted regions. The result of this signal separation is a super-position of map structures, yielding sharp boundaries at the occultation region. We introduce a model that penalizes the harmonic complexity of the model map with Tikhonov regularization, whose parameters are tuned to reproduce the fit quality of the eigenmapping model. We use JWST NIRSpec/PRISM full-orbit observations of the eclipsing WD 1202-024 system as a template to construct and run injection-recovery tests on simulated light curves, isolating both latitudinal structures as well as emission from a physically-realistic general circulation model (GCM). In the latter, the narrow equatorial jet driven by the BD's rapid rotation manifests as an eclipse depth asymmetry, which our model reproduces as a latitude-dependent phase offset. Such a model, however, is only statistically preferred at approximately $3 \times$ the signal-to-noise ratio of the JWST data. When fitting to the actual JWST data of WD 1202, the full-phase eigenbasis model is statistically preferred. However, the resulting model map of WD 1202 B does not resemble the GCM predictions, with a concentrated day-side hotspot at the sub-stellar point with an angular size $\approx 15^\circ$. Interpreting this result more carefully requires follow-up work to disentangle systematics from true emission signals. This model framework provides a means to detect emission features from these rare types of eclipses, and ultimately to test predictions of models of atmospheric circulation across hot Jupiters and their BD analogs.

2610.36201.title: Measuring masses of transiting Earth-like planets: first insights from the PLATO RV data challenge

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration in the ($K$,$P$) parameter space of the three multi-planetary systems injected in the HARPS-N solar data: A (blue), B (orange) and C (green). Transiting planets are depicted with a round marker (see legend). All the transiting planets in this work were smaller than $7\hbox{$\mathrm{M}_{\oplus}$}$. Four isomasses lines are indicated. The 2470 exoplanets with a measured semi-amplitude according to NASA exoplanet archive are represented as a comparison.

Figure 2: Illustration of the GLS periodogram for the three data set A1050 (top panel), B1300 (middle panel) and C800 (bottom panel) without the planets injected. Although the GLS is traditionally represented in terms of power, we display it here in $K$ semi-amplitude sinusoids scaling to facilitate a direct comparison with the semi-amplitudes of the injected signals. Transiting planets are shown in green (mono-transit in orange), non-transiting one in red. Signals larger than 3 m/s are just truncated and their marker is replaced by an upper arrow. We also indicate above each marker the ratio of the planetary amplitude with the native GLS power at the same period.

Figure 3: Representation of the main time-series provided for the RV challenge. Top panel: RV time-series (YV0) of the A1300 (blue), B1050 (orange) and C800 (green) data sets. Arbitrary vertical offset were applied for graphical considerations. Middle panel: The plage filling factor as extracted from the MgII index and converted here in plage filling factor using the reference time-series of Cretignier et al. (2024b). Bottom panel: Total solar irradiance converted here from usual $W/m^{2}$ units to ppm by using solar minimum flux level as reference.

Figure 4: Representation of the RV budget expected from the main solar components in the PLATO RV challenge that uses the solar HARPS-N data set. A time serie of eight years including 15 minutes of integration time was generated using the ARVE code using the solar atmospheric parameters (only one rotational period is shown here). The contribution from each component is indicated in the legend with from top to bottom: the photon noise (15 cm/s), p-mode oscillation (5 cm/s), granulation (24 cm/s), supergranulation (62 cm/s) and their sum (86 cm/s).

Figure 5: Representation of the $K_{i}$ semi-amplitude posterior for the six injected planets of the A1050 data set for each participant. Black vertical line was the ground truth $K_{\text{inj}}$, while 10% and 25% levels are indicated by the vertical dashed-dotted and dotted lines respectively. All the panels with a score better than 25% are displayed in yellow box, while all the scores better than 10% are in green. Planets missed are showed with a black frame. Each panel also indicates the accuracy and the number of sigma $N_{\sigma}$. If $N_{\sigma}$ is smaller than 2, the value is highlighted in bold. For most participants all the planets are constrained down to 10%. The most difficult signal of the A1050 data set is the HZ transiting signal at 373 days for which no participant get a 10% score and the mass tend to be overestimated. We do not see any peculiar issue for the transiting planet closed to the solar rotation period.

Figure 6: Representation of the pair accuracy  and precision  for each injected signal correctly detected by the participants for the data set A1050. Participants are represented with the same symbols as in Fig.5. The 10% PLATO requirement is indicated with a green dashed square, the 25% score is shown with the orange dashed-dotted square. Any dot inside the square satisfy the score requirement. The black solid box represents the score of the benchmark (see Sect.2.3.1). The 1 and 2-$\sigma$ are shown by the cone plain lines.

Figure 7: Same as Fig.6 for the data set B1300. All the participants underestimated the mass of the inner most and outermost planets. If the outermost period was not constrained since the case of a mono-transit. The underestimation of the inner one is more difficult to understand. No participant except one, detected the non-transiting 187-day planet.
Figure 8: Same as Fig.6 for the data set C800. With among the smallest amplitudes, no participants manages to reach 25% precision on the transiting terrestrial planets.

Figure 9: Representation of the maximum error $\varepsilon_{K}$ obtained by all the participants on each injected planetary signal. Each participant is represented by a row and its unique assigned color/marker combination. The participants are ordered by their average maximum error  on the terrestrial signal category, but this ordering does not represent a ranking (see plain text Sect.3.3). The exact planetary signal is indicated in the bottom axis label by its system and orbital period (as well as ’T’ transit indication). The planetary signals were ordered by the maximum error obtained by the benchmark (first row). The false positive detections are indicated on the left part of the vertical green line. The scale of the colorbar was set such as the 25% level is white, better score will be blue, worse red. A missed signal (true negative) is represented by a black box.

Figure 10: Average maximum error $\varepsilon_{k}$ for the 16 injected planets. Four different subsets were analysed (from top to bottom panels): terrestrial planets, the transiting planets, the habitable-zone (HZ) transiting planets and the full sample of planets. Each participant is represented by the same marker as in Fig.9. Participants names are however not displayed since this metric alone is not sufficient to allow for a ranking (see plain text).
The two arbitrary levels defined in this challenge are also displayed as horizontal lines at 10% (green dashed line) and 25% (orange dashed-dotted line).

2610.36201.abstract:
The PLATO Stellar Variability Mitigation Working Group designed a radial-velocity (RV) data challenge to assess the precision and accuracy achievable on RV semi-amplitudes in the context of the future PLATO follow-up.
Using Sun-as-a-star observations obtained with HARPS-N, we generated three multi-planet systems with realistic sampling, an effective signal-to-noise ratio of S/N ~ 450, an exposure time of 15 minutes, and a total of approximately 1000 observations. The resulting data set is publicly available and can serve as a benchmark for the community to test and compare RV analysis methods. Eight independent teams participated in the challenge, aiming to recover the semi-amplitudes of both transiting and non-transiting planets.
A meta-analysis of the submitted results shows that, with current data analysis methods, HARPS-N-like stability and the observing strategy studied in this paper, achieving a precision on semi-amplitudes better than 10% for habitable-zone signals around a solar-type star is challenging, and is typically limited to planets with masses of approximately 8-10 Earth masses. This performance is expected to improve for K dwarfs, where planets down to approximately 2-5 Earth masses may be characterized at a similar level of precision.
Finally, based on the results of this challenge and the occurrence of false positives, we derive an empirical detection threshold for RV surveys, which can be used to distinguish robust planetary detections from candidates.

2610.36446.title: Retention of primordial atmospheres through giant impacts

figures.caption: Figure 1: Atmospheric evolution with and without a post-disk giant impact. Panel 1: The common initial state for a rocky planet with a hydrogen-rich atmosphere. Panels 2a–4a: A giant impact deposits energy into the mantle and core, but the increase in gravitational binding energy dominates, allowing the planet to retain its hydrogen-rich atmosphere and evolve into a sub-Neptune ($1.75{-}3.5~R_{\oplus}$). Panels 2b–4b: In the absence of such an impact, the planet is less massive, loses its primordial atmosphere under sustained stellar irradiation, and becomes a super-Earth ($1{-}1.75~R_{\oplus}$).

Figure 2: Bimodal exoplanet radius distributions under different giant-impact assumptions. Panels (a,b), (c,d), and (e,f) use the power-law, Pareto, and logarithmic distributions of the impactor-to-final-planet mass ratio defined by Equations 11, 12, and 13, respectively. The left and right columns assume post-disk giant impact probabilities of $52\%$ and $74\%$, respectively, based on N-body simulations [6, 5]. The metallic core mass fraction is uniformly distributed from 10% to 40% (based on constraints set by stellar elemental ratios [43] and rocky exoplanet densities [44]), and the atmospheric mass fraction scales with nucleus mass according to Equation 5. The initial exoplanet mass distribution is shown in Figure 4a. Dark-red step curves and pale-red shading show the probability-density distributions of the final radii of $10^{8}$ synthetic planets. Black circles and vertical bars show the completeness-corrected occurrence in each radius bin and corresponding $1\sigma$ uncertainties from Ref. [1], each divided by the area under the binned occurrence distribution. The uncertainties are derived from Poisson counting statistics and scaled using simulated transit surveys. Horizontal bars show a fixed $\pm 0.2\,R_{\oplus}$ approximation to the typical radius uncertainty illustrated in Figure 7 of Ref. [1].

Figure 3: Probability of complete atmospheric loss after giant impacts. The colour scale shows the probability of total atmospheric loss as a function of the impactor-to-final-planet mass ratio, $\chi$, and initial planetary mass, $M_{\rm ini}$. White curves mark probability contours of 0.01, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50, 0.70, and 0.80. This figure was generated using a sample size of $10^{8}$ synthetic planets. The red dashed line shows the analytic approximation for the impactor-to-final-planet mass ratio required for 1% of all planets of initial mass $M_{\rm ini}$ to experience total atmospheric loss.

Figure 4: Adopted initial mass distribution and corresponding radii without atmospheric loss. (a) The mass distribution of exoplanets adopted in this study. The core of Saturn ($15{-}18~M_{\oplus}$ [107, 108]) and one of the largest observed rocky exoplanet candidates, Kepler-277 b ($87^{{+}42}_{{-}40}~M_{\oplus}$ [109, 110]), are shown for reference. The line at $25~M_{\oplus}$ marks the suggested rocky mass limit proposed by [111]. (b) The radius distribution of our synthetic exoplanet population at 5 Gyr, assuming no atmospheric loss occurs.

Figure 5: Mantle thermodynamics and impact-energy partitioning. (a) The adiabats for a $10~M_{\oplus}$ planet with a metallic core mass fraction of 0.325 at 2500 K, 3000 K, 3500 K, 4000 K, 4500 K, and 5000 K. The solidus, rheological transition ($\phi{=}0.4$), and liquidus are shown in black. (b) The fraction of impact energy deposited to the mantle, $\Delta E/\left(\Delta E{+}\Delta E_{\rm c}\right)$, as a function of the metallic core mass fraction $f_{\rm c}$.

Figure 6: Post-impact surface temperatures. The post-impact surface temperature ($T_{\rm sur}$; Equation 34) as a function of the ratio of the impactor’s mass over the final planetary mass ($\chi$) and the planetary nuclear mass ($M_{\rm n}$) for a planet with an Earth-like metallic core mass fraction. White dashed curves mark the labeled temperature contours.

Extended Figure 1: Adopted giant-impact size distributions. The power-law, Pareto, and logarithmic distributions are shown by the green solid, red dashed, and blue dotted curves and are defined by Equations 11, 12, and 13, respectively.

Extended Figure 2: Bimodal radius distributions under alternative giant-impact and cooling assumptions. The points with error bars represent observational data [1]. Horizontal uncertainties are approximated from “typical uncert” in Figure 7 of Ref. [1]. Panels (a–c) show results using a $63\%$ impact probability with (a) a power-law, (b) a Pareto, and (c) a logarithmic distribution in $\chi$ (Equations 11–13). Panels (d$-$f) adopt a uniform distribution in $\chi$ with post-disk impact probabilities of $52\%$, $63\%$, and $74\%$, respectively. Panels (g$-$i) adopt a uniform distribution in $\chi$. Panels (g) and (h) correspond to post-disk giant impact probabilities of 0% and 100%, respectively. Panel (i) corresponds to a 63% post-disk impact probability, with the magma ocean cooling time $t_{\rm cool}$ set equal to the total planetary age, $t_{\rm age}{=}5~{\rm Gyr}$. Dark-red step curves and pale-red shading show the probability-density distributions of the final radii of $10^{8}$ synthetic planets. Black circles and vertical bars show the completeness-corrected occurrence in each radius bin and corresponding $1\sigma$ uncertainties from Ref. [1], each divided by the area under the binned occurrence distribution. The uncertainties are derived from Poisson counting statistics and scaled using simulated transit surveys. Horizontal bars show a fixed $\pm 0.2\,R_{\oplus}$ approximation to the typical radius uncertainty illustrated in Figure 7 of Ref. [1].

2610.36446.abstract: Rocky planets the size of Earth or larger are expected to undergo one or more giant impacts during the final stages of their formation. Some of these collisions occur after protoplanetary disk dissipation, potentially driving the loss of primordial hydrogen-rich atmospheres through elevated surface temperatures. However, whether giant impacts promote atmospheric loss or retention remains unclear because they both heat planetary interiors and increase atmospheric gravitational binding. Here we model the evolution of rocky planets after their largest post-disk giant impact, accounting self-consistently for the concurrent increase in gravitational binding energy and mantle thermal energy. Whereas the entire accreted mass contributes to the increase in gravitational binding energy, only part of the impact energy raises mantle temperature. Mantle melting consumes energy as latent heat, while the impactor's metallic core transfers little energy to the mantle and remains superheated at depth. Giant impacts therefore increase gravitational binding energy more than mantle thermal energy, shifting planets towards atmospheric retention. Larger, atmosphere-bearing planets emerge preferentially through collisional growth. By contrast, smaller planets without such impacts tend to lose their primordial atmospheres under sustained stellar irradiation. At the population level, these results suggest that sub-Neptunes have, on average, more massive rocky interiors than super-Earths.

2610.36664.title: Revisiting the Photometric Modulation Amplitudes of Kepler Planet Hosts: A Confounder-Adjusted Test of Stellar Spin-Orbit Alignment

figures.caption: Figure 1: Sky-projected stellar obliquity $\lambda$ as a function of host-star effective temperature for planets with orbital periods $P<100\,\mathrm{days}$. From top to bottom, the panels show systems with $R_{p}<4\,R_{\oplus}$, $4\,R_{\oplus}<R_{p}<8\,R_{\oplus}$, and $R_{p}>8\,R_{\oplus}$. The obliquities, stellar effective temperatures, orbital periods, and published planetary radii are compiled from TEPCat [61]; the horizontal and vertical error bars show the cataloged uncertainties in $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $\lambda$, respectively, where available. This is a heterogeneous compilation rather than a uniformly selected sample, and the measurements differ in precision and reliability. Accordingly, this figure is intended to illustrate the current state of the available measurements rather than to support a statistical inference about the underlying obliquity distributions. The giant-planet sample spans a wide range of obliquities but also shows a pronounced concentration of aligned systems near $\lambda=0^{\circ}$, extending up to $T_{\mathrm{eff}}\sim 6500\,\mathrm{K}$ [65].
Figure 2: The Kepler magnitude distributions of KIC (black solid) and KOI (orange dotted) stars in the 44 sample.

Both analyses use KIC reference densities weighted by the detectability of transiting planets, $\pi_{\mathrm{D|TR}}$. Positive values indicate larger amplitudes for KOIs.

Figure 10: The inferred $\alpha(T_{\mathrm{eff}})$ for all KOIs (orange dotted curve) and for two equal-sized subsamples divided by the orbital period of the innermost planet candidate: $P_{\rm inner}<8.6\,\mathrm{days}$ (salmon stars) and $P_{\rm inner}>8.6\,\mathrm{days}$ (blue squares). The shaded regions show the 16th–84th percentile intervals for the two subsamples. For each subsample, the KIC reference density was trained using $\pi_{\mathrm{D|TR}}$ marginalized over the corresponding period range of the simulated planet population.

2610.36664.abstract: T. Mazeh and coworkers pioneered a method using rotational photometric modulation as a proxy to infer stellar obliquities in Kepler transiting planetary systems, based on the expected positive correlation between spot-induced modulation amplitudes and stellar inclinations. They found that planet hosts cooler than the Sun showed larger modulation amplitudes than comparison stars, consistent with low stellar obliquities. For hotter hosts, however, they reported the opposite - a negative amplitude difference (hosts minus comparison stars) - which is difficult to interpret in terms of viewing geometry. We show that this comparison is affected by confounding variables not controlled for in the sample selection. One such confounder is apparent magnitude, whose distributions differ markedly between the two samples for hotter stars and affect the observed modulation amplitudes. We develop resampling and likelihood-based approaches that enable comparison of the amplitude distributions at fixed apparent magnitude, stellar radius, and rotation period. The previously reported negative amplitude difference for hot hosts is no longer present in either analysis. The likelihood-based analysis finds a positive amplitude difference up to $\sim 6100\,\mathrm{K}$ that becomes consistent with zero at higher temperatures, while the resampling analysis shows a similar but less pronounced trend. This result is qualitatively consistent with independent $v\sin i$ analyses suggesting low obliquities for cooler super-Earth and sub-Neptune hosts and broader obliquity distributions for hotter ones. This may also indicate a gradual change in the obliquity distribution with stellar temperature, although changes in spot distributions or selection effects could also contribute to the photometric trends in hot stars.

2610.36979.abstract: Venus is home to vivid sulfur chemistry, with SO$_2$ as the major sulfur gas species and a global cloud layer between 47 and~70 km composed of H$_2$SO$_4$ and H$_2$O. The chemistry in the clouds has been extensively studied with 1D models, but none is able to reproduce the three orders of magnitude decrease of SO$_2$ inside the clouds. Sulfur allotrope chemistry could be a candidate for buffering sulfur atoms, as it can grow into long chains. Sulfur hydrides such as H$_2$S is considered as one of the main sulfur-bearing compounds, possibly linked to surface reactions or have a volcanic origin like on Earth. In this study, we use for the first time a 3D model to study the climatology of the sulfur allotrope in gas and condensed phase and hydride chemistry in the clouds with an explicit photolysis calculation and updated UV cross-section. H$_2$S is close to ppmv levels below the cloud base, the third most abundant sulfur-bearing species in this region after SO$_2$ and OCS. Below the clouds, S$_8$ gas phase is the most abundant sulfur allotrope. Above, the photolysis and condensation are preponderant, and the gas phase decreases to extremely low values. Polysulfur can therefore not be the unknown absorber at cloud-top altitudes. The condensed phase polysulfurs are present from 30 to above 100~km. S$_2$ condensed phase is the most abundant due to its low saturation mixing ratios. Polysulfur species represent a substantial sulfur reservoir in the upper cloud, equivalent to a few ppmv.

2610.37004.title: Unbound grains in gaseous debris discs

figures.caption: Figure 1: Sketch of the system, showing the star (yellow circle), gas disc (blue), and planetesimal belt (black circle) in which the unbound grains (grey) are produced. The gas may or may not extend much further inwards from the planetesimal belt; this is irrelevant for the unbound grains, which only move outwards.

Figure 2: Radial velocity as a function of radius for dust grains of three different sizes (see panel titles) in a disc with no gas and in gaseous discs with three different gas masses (different colours; see plot legend). Solid lines show the results of numerical integration of the equations of motion, while dashed lines show the analytical model. The particles with $\beta=0.55$ become bound if the gas is sufficiently massive. In these cases (orange and green curves in the right-hand panel), the curves wrap around multiple times as the particles repeatedly oscillate radially inwards and outwards along eccentric orbits. Periods during which the particles move inwards (negative radial velocity) are not shown because of the logarithmic axis. The curves wrap around progressively more tightly as the orbits slowly circularize. We show the equilibrium radii at which these particles would settle given sufficient time as vertical dotted lines. The gas is assumed to be composed primarily of molecular hydrogen.

Figure 3: Contribution of unbound grains to the disc surface brightness in scattered light at 1 µm as function of radius, from the numerical model (solid lines) and an analytical model (dashed lines). The values are normalised so that the surface brightness at 100 au is equal to one in the low-gas-mass limit. Left: Gas is assumed to be composed primarily of CO. Right: Gas is assumed to be composed primarily of molecular hydrogen and to have a much higher mass.
Figure 4: Same as Fig. 3 but for thermal emission at 12 µm.

2610.37004.abstract: Context. Some debris discs contain cold molecular gas. The origin of this gas is one of the key questions in our understanding of the evolution of planetary systems. The effect of gas on the smallest dust grains, which are expected to be unbound due to radiation pressure, is not well understood. The unbound grains contribute to the brightness of scattered light and thermal emission from the disc halo at short wavelengths. Aims. We explored the conditions under which gas can prevent or slow down the escape of unbound grains and increase their number density in the disc halo sufficiently to affect its brightness and reveal properties of the gas. Methods. We numerically integrated the equations of motion of dust grains released on unbound orbits in optically thin, gaseous debris discs, taking into account stellar gravity, radiation pressure, Poynting-Robertson drag, and gas drag. Results. We find that gas drag can significantly slow down the escape of unbound grains only for very high gas masses, such as those expected if the gas is remnant protoplanetary gas and not of secondary origin. We also present an analytical model for estimating the density of unbound grains in gaseous discs. Conclusions. If a difference in the abundance of unbound grains between gaseous and non-gaseous debris discs were observed, it would imply that the gas in debris discs is protoplanetary. Currently, there is no evidence of such a difference, suggesting that the gas detected in debris discs is either secondary or strongly depleted protoplanetary gas.

A vertical line at 8.25 µm marks the location of a feature in the 17P and 73P spectra, a line at 9.3 µm marks the normalization point, lines at 9.95 and 11.15 µm mark the locations of Mg-rich crystalline olivine features in the spectra of 17P and 73P.

The colors show solutions within $\Delta\ln P>$ -10, -5, and -2 of the best-fitting model. The relationship between silicate abundance and silicate peak grain size is clear across a space of high-probability solutions.

Figure 4: Left: The calculated ridge of solutions through the $\log_{10}(\mathrm{sil}/\mathrm{car})$ versus $a_{p,\mathrm{sil}}$ parameter space. Solutions A-E correspond to the 10th, 30th, 50th, 70th,
and 90th percentiles in $a_{p,\rm sil}$ among solutions with
$\Delta\ln P>-5$. Right: 3I/ATLAS emissivity spectrum compared to the modeled spectra for solutions A-E. All solutions are reasonable fits to the silicate emissivity feature. Our dust model does not include the emission feature observed at 6.83 $\mu$m.

2610.37540.abstract: We present JWST/MIRI Low Resolution Spectroscopy (LRS) of 3I/ATLAS obtained post-perihelion at a heliocentric distance of 2.21 au. Our spectrum contains a prominent 10 micron silicate emission feature with a broad, smooth shape that is distinct from those commonly observed in Solar System comets. We model the spectrum using thermal emission from amorphous carbon, amorphous olivine, and amorphous pyroxene grains. Our models strongly favor a pyroxene-dominated, amorphous silicate composition and show a degeneracy between silicate grain size and the relative abundance of silicate and carbon dust. Across a set of representative models, the best-fitting crystalline abundance is zero, and we place an upper limit of 5.3% on the crystalline fraction of the silicates. We identify an emission feature near 6.83 microns that is consistent with aliphatic C-H-bearing material. The overwhelmingly amorphous silicate composition supports previous work that measured unusual volatile and isotopic composition in suggesting that the material incorporated into the object experienced little thermal processing and preserves information about the conditions in which this interstellar planetesimal formed.

2610.36200.abstract: We assess how propulsion and operational constraints affect exo-Earth characterization with a starshade rendezvous mission for a Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO)-like telescope at Sun-Earth L2. Using end-to-end Monte Carlo simulations with EXOSIMS, we model a 60 m starshade for visible-band spectroscopy (500-1000 nm) and a 35 m starshade for near-ultraviolet characterization (250-550 nm). For the 60 m design, we compare AEPS Hall, NEXT ion, and Starlink-class Hall thrusters and examine sensitivity to propellant capacity, the fraction of each retargeting slew spent accelerating and decelerating, and on-orbit refueling. With 1000-3000 kg of initial propellant and no refueling, NEXT provides the highest characterization yield: 9-13% more characterizations than AEPS and 13-16% more than the Starlink-class option. Its higher specific impulse enables more retargeting slews per kilogram of propellant. With refueling, yields converge across thruster choices to about 120 cumulative characterizations over 10 years, while propulsion choice mainly affects the number of refueling events. For the 35 m starshade with AEPS, yields are less sensitive to fuel and are dominated by mission duration and geometric accessibility. Increasing the minimum solar keepout angle from 40 to 50 degrees has little effect on yield; increases from 50 to 65 degrees have a modest effect, while angles above 65 degrees rapidly reduce yield, with severe degradation near 80 degrees. These results distinguish fuel-limited and time- or keepout-limited regimes and guide propulsion selection, tank sizing, refueling policy, and keepout constraints for HWO starshade missions.

2610.36315.title: Calculation of distant retrograde orbits and their use in space weather forecasting

Both a linear and a 2nd order polynomial fit are shown. (b) Solutions for 11 DROs with steps of 0.02 au, from 0.74 to 0.94 au, in an HEE coordinate system in which the Earth is at $x,y=(1,0)$ au. We assume a minimum of 4 spacecraft.

Figure 7: Illustration of our definition of far upstream monitoring and sub-L1 monitoring, with Venus acting as the discriminator between the two regimes. A distant retrograde orbit for the SHIELD concept, with a minimum distance of 0.86 au, is given as an orange solid line. Another concept is introduced as the blue solid lines, which shows the points for which the distance to the Sun–Earth line ($L_{s}$) is similar as the distance to 1 au ($R_{s}$). We call this the RLD $=0$ line, meaning the radial to longitude spatial scale difference is 0. The line discriminates the domains for which radial evolution of an ICME matters more (RLD $>0$) and the domain for which the longitudinal structure of an ICME is of higher importance (RLD $<0$). A “cone of acceptance,” with an assumed width of $\Lambda$ of 15°, is indicated too.

2610.36315.abstract: There is current renewed interest in using Sun-Earth distant retrograde orbits (DROs) for a space weather forecasting mission, which would temporarily place spacecraft at a position near the Sun-Earth line, but closer to the Sun than the L1 point (such as the ESA HENON mission and ESA SHIELD concept). With in situ observations of the magnetic field on a DRO, the southward ($B_z < 0$) magnetic field of interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs), which is not routinely accessible remotely, could be measured several hours in advance. This $B_z < 0$ field is a decisive factor for forecasting geomagnetic storm intensity. We present an analysis of DROs at different sub-L1 distances for their efficacy for a space weather forecasting mission. An open-source numerical framework to generate DRO trajectories is presented. Our pre-calculated orbits in Heliocentric Earth Ecliptic coordinates can be introduced into numerical or empirical simulations of the ambient solar wind and ICMEs. We then analyze the corresponding forecast lead times, the resulting observational gaps depending on the number of spacecraft and distance of a DRO, and the "cone of acceptance" of the maximum longitudinal separation of a spacecraft to the Sun-Earth line. We define different domains regarding radial evolution and longitudinal CME structure, and show the historical coverage of sub-L1 ICME observations with our ICMECAT catalog. An optimal mission configuration can be selected based on the characteristics of DROs presented here, depending on the requirements of such a mission deemed acceptable with respect to results on CME evolution and coherence.

2610.36336.abstract: We report the discovery of periodic radio bursts from the T8 brown dwarf WISE J151721.13+052929.3 (WISE J1517+05), detected with ASKAP and MeerKAT. The emission is characterised by a stable periodicity of $1.149 \pm 0.002$ hr, placing WISE J1517+05 among the fastest rotating radio-detected ultracool dwarfs (UCDs). The radio bursts are broadband and highly variable, reaching a peak spectral luminosity of $L_{u} = 5.6 \times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$, making WISE J1517+05 the brightest periodic UCD to date. The high brightness temperature of the radio bursts ($T_B>10^{11}$ K), combined with the rotational modulation, strongly favour an auroral electron cyclotron maser emission (ECME) origin. In contrast to most known radio-bursting UCDs, the bursts exhibit relatively low and variable circular polarisation fractions (typically $\sim 20\%$). These properties suggest significant depolarisation of intrinsically highly polarised ECME, likely due to propagation effects in a structured magnetospheric plasma. Notably, we also observe a polarisation reversal within a single burst profile, which is currently unexplained. We model the emission using a dipolar magnetic field with emission arising from a single active field line, and find a moderate inclination angle of $i = 47.9^{+11.4}_{-9.2}$ degrees and a magnetic obliquity of $\beta = 40.1^{+9.2}_{-10.9}$ degrees. WISE J1517+05 expands the parameter space of radio-active UCDs toward higher luminosities and lower polarisation fractions, suggesting that current surveys may be sensitive to a larger population than previously recognised, while searches relying on methods that assume high circular polarisation fractions risk missing a subset of UCDs. More broadly, this discovery reinforces the idea that rapid rotation plays a key role in generating strong dipolar magnetic fields in UCDs that can give rise to auroral radio emission.
